instructions: Read the original passage and choose one answer for each question.
passage:
In the fictional town of Brookfield, a community kitchen is planning a Saturday demonstration. The chef who leads it, Mara, wants visitors to learn the names of tools and to ask clear questions about food. The event is not a restaurant service. The small group will watch, talk and then help arrange a table. They agree to ask before borrowing a tool and to return it when they have finished. This gives the next person room to work. Anyone with a food question can ask the staff before choosing a portion.

Mara puts an apron on before the visitors arrive at ten thirty. She asks them to wash their hands and gives each person a card. The card which has a green corner lists the vegetarian menu. Another card describes a dish that contains milk. The cards are used to start a conversation, not to guarantee that every ingredient is suitable for every visitor. Mara invites anyone who needs more information to speak with the staff.

On the table there is a pot, a spoon, a knife and a fork. A tray stands near the sink. Mara will measure the ingredients before she begins. She places raw vegetables in one bowl and explains which knife belongs on the table. A ripe tomato goes into a second bowl. She asks a volunteer to read the label on a jar of powder; the label gives the name, but the group will ask if they need further details.

The menu offers a mild sauce made with yogurt. Visitors can describe the flavor as sweet, sour or spicy according to what they taste; Mara does not insist that everyone use the same word. The mixture has a smooth texture, while the roasted vegetables feel different. One guest says the aroma is delicious, but another prefers a less strong smell. Their comments describe preferences rather than a rule about which food is best.

Mara shows three ways to prepare a vegetable. The group can roast it in an oven, grill it on a pan, or steam it in a covered pot. A different sauce will simmer while the group talks. She does not ask visitors to copy a technique at home without checking their own equipment and instructions. Instead, she demonstrates how to describe each step with a clear sentence.

At the end, visitors place a small portion on a plate if they wish. The room where they eat has seats beside a wide window. Mara writes down one suggestion for the next event: invite a guest who can describe another cuisine. The group thanks the chef and returns the tools to the table. They leave with a short menu and a list of questions they can use when joining another shared meal.
